transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
A major nor'easter is making its way up the coast,
disrupting Thanksgiving travel plans and holiday events.
In New York City, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been moved to Saturday,
the first time it's been postponed in its 100-year history.
Mayor Zoran Mamdani says the city made the decision
to protect the people taking part in the parade and the crowds along the route.
This decision, as you heard, was made in coordination with Macy's,
the NYPD, and many agency partners.
Safety is and will always remain our top priority,
and this will be a heavy storm.
We are expecting sustained winds between 30 and 40 miles per hour,
with gusts as high as 60 to 65 miles per hour possible.
On the West Coast, unusually high tides are prompting coastal flood warnings.
In Northern California, evacuation orders and warnings
have been issued for several communities.
Jefferson Public Radio's Theo Greenlee reports.
Residents of the small waterfront community of King Salmon
were ordered to evacuate Tuesday as rising water flooded local streets.
But a day later, Eli Blassingame was still in his trailer at a local RV park
where he's lived for three years, even as floodwaters rose.
It went probably up to my thigh, the water did,
so I had to start putting on hip waders because the tide was coming in.
The National Weather Service says unusually high tides, El Nino,
and strong southerly winds have pushed water levels near historic highs.
Forecasters say flooding remains possible through Friday.
For NPR News, I'm Theo Greenlee in Beaverton.
The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on imports from 14 trading partners,
including China, Japan, and the European Union.
Most Chinese goods would face an additional 20 percent tariff.
The stock market ended mixed today after some big swings earlier.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports investors got both good news and bad news
from the Commerce Department.
A fresh gross domestic product report from the Commerce Department
says the U.S. economy grew even faster than initially thought
in July, August, and September.
GDP grew at an annual rate of 4.3 percent in the third quarter.
That's the strongest showing in three years,
fueled by robust consumer spending
and the massive investment in artificial intelligence.
Faster growth comes with an unwelcome side effect, however,
higher inflation prices in October were up 3.8 percent from a year ago,
according to the Commerce Department's inflation gauge,
which is closely tracked by the Federal Reserve.
The Fed is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate next month
in an effort to bring prices under control.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News.
Scientists have identified what could be a new way
to spot the chance of a woman getting pregnant.
The findings focus on the male's contribution to fertility.
They were published in proceedings
of the National Academy of Sciences this week.
NPR's Will Stone reports.
The study from researchers at Wayne State University
looked at more than 300 men with seemingly normal sperm
and homed in on what's known as mitochondrial DNA.
The genetic material for mitochondria, which produce energy
and carry out many functions in our cells,
is passed down through the mother.
But the study's lead author, Richard Pilsner,
says they see that men with sperm that have greater concentrations
of this mitochondrial DNA also have a much higher chance
of not being able to get pregnant with their partners.
Those men that have presumably normal semen parameters,
this molecular signature is tracking with probability of pregnancy.
It's not clear why this is the case,
but Pilsner says the goal is to come up with more precise ways
to measure male fertility.
Will Stone, NPR News.
Lawmakers in Australia have passed a law requiring tech companies
to identify and reduce risks to users.
The rules cover online games, apps and AI chatbots.
Companies that violate the law could face fines
of up to 5% of their global revenue.
The Australian government says companies need to address risks
from the way their products are designed
as well as the content people see.
The US Ambassador to Australia warns the threat of steep fines
could lead companies to take down lawful speech.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York moved to Saturday due to nor'easter
Unusually high tides prompt flood warnings and evacuation orders in Northern California's King Salmon
Trump administration proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, Japan, and EU
Third-quarter GDP grows 4.3 percent, but October inflation rises to 3.8 percent
Study links higher mitochondrial DNA in sperm to lower chance of pregnancy, from Wayne State University
Australia passes law requiring tech companies to reduce risks to users, with fines up to 5%
